section: 5.5 Train a Support Vector Regression Model
text:
5.5 Train a Support Vector Regression Model
Purpose: Fit a kernel-based model that is robust to high-dimensional data and captures non-linear boundaries via the radial basis function (RBF), after scaling the predictors.

# Scale predictors before training
predictors <- c("smoking_prev", "obesity_prev", "diabetes_prev",
                "alcohol_per_capita", "family_history_prev",
                "urbanization_pct", "TOTPOP")
ml_data_scaled <- ml_data |> 
  mutate(across(all_of(predictors), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))


svr_model <- train_svr(
  data = ml_data,
  formula = rf_formula
)

print(svr_model)


Call:
svm(formula = formula, data = data, type = "eps-regression", kernel = "radial")


Parameters:
   SVM-Type:  eps-regression 
 SVM-Kernel:  radial 
       cost:  1 
      gamma:  0.1428571 
    epsilon:  0.1 


Number of Support Vectors:  49








NoteWhat Support Vector Regression is



SVR fits a function that is flat — within a margin (ε) it tolerates errors, and it only cares about points outside that margin (the support vectors). The radial (RBF) kernel lets it capture non-linear relationships by mapping points into a higher-dimensional space without doing the maths explicitly.
Two things to note from the summary:

Number of support vectors — here about 49 of the 54 rows, which is typical for small, noisy datasets: the model cannot find a simple structure, so nearly every point ends up supporting the fit.
The predictors are scaled first (scale() gives each a mean of 0 and SD of 1), because the RBF kernel is distance-based.



Key parameters: - train_svr() uses the radial kernel by default (kernel = "radial" in e1071::svm()). - Tuning cost and gamma via cross-validation (e.g., caret::train()) is recommended for production models. - scale() standardises each predictor to a mean of 0, SD of 1. - as.numeric strips the matrix class of the scale() output into a clean numeric column.
Expected output: An svm summary showing the number of support vectors and model parameters. The number of support vectors is fairly high for a 54-row dataset, which is normal for small datasets.

5.6 Evaluate Model Performance
Purpose: Compare models using standardized accuracy metrics: RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), MAE (Mean Absolute Error), and R² (coefficient of determination).

# Generate in-sample predictions from each model and compute RMSE/MAE/R2
# using caret::postResample()

# Random Forest predictions
rf_preds <- predict(rf_model, newdata = ml_data)
rf_metrics <- postResample(pred = rf_preds, obs = ml_data$incidence_rate)

# XGBoost predictions
xgb_preds <- predict(xgb_model, newdata = as.matrix(ml_data[, predictors]))
xgb_metrics <- postResample(pred = xgb_preds, obs = ml_data$incidence_rate)

# SVR predictions (on the scaled predictor set used for training)
svr_preds <- predict(svr_model, newdata = ml_data_scaled)
svr_metrics <- postResample(pred = svr_preds, obs = ml_data$incidence_rate)

# Combine into a comparison table
model_eval <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVR"),
  RMSE = c(rf_metrics["RMSE"], xgb_metrics["RMSE"], svr_metrics["RMSE"]),
  MAE  = c(rf_metrics["MAE"], xgb_metrics["MAE"], svr_metrics["MAE"]),
  Rsquared = c(rf_metrics["Rsquared"], xgb_metrics["Rsquared"], svr_metrics["Rsquared"])
)

model_eval[order(model_eval$RMSE), ]

          Model       RMSE        MAE   Rsquared
2       XGBoost 0.06760268 0.05110464 0.99961714
1 Random Forest 1.35280160 0.99251357 0.92853411
3           SVR 2.86476363 1.94351030 0.01138557








NoteThe three metrics




RMSE — square root of the mean squared error; penalises large errors more, and is in the same units as the outcome.
MAE — mean absolute error; the average size of an error, easy to interpret.
R² — the proportion of variance explained (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than predicting the mean).

caret::postResample(pred, obs) computes all three from predictions and the true values.


Key parameters: - predict(): Requires a newdata to supply the predictor variables to generate predictions for a particular model. - postResample() compares the predicted values against ground truth (the target variable, incidence_rate) to generate standard regression performance metrics.
Expected output: A three-row data frame ranking the models.






WarningIn-sample ≠ generalisation



These are in-sample (training-set) metrics: every model is evaluated on the very data it was trained on. A high R² here means the model memorised the training data, not that it learned a real relationship. Tree-based models in particular (especially XGBoost with enough rounds) can fit training data almost perfectly even when the true relationship is weak or non-existent — exactly the scenario we have with our uncorrelated simulated covariates. A high in-sample R² is not evidence of a real relationship; it is a reminder of why we need held-out cross-validation, which the next section does.

set.seed(222)

cv_control <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5,

rf_cv <- train(

# Manually cross-validate XGBoost using xgb.cv
# (current version of xgboost breaks with caret::train)
xgb_matrix_full <- xgb.DMatrix(
  data  = as.matrix(ml_data[, predictors]),
  label = ml_data$incidence_rate
)

xgb_cv <- xgb.cv(
  data = xgb_matrix_full,
  params = list(
    objective = "reg:squarederror",
    max_depth = 4,
    eta = 0.1
  ),
  metrics = list("rmse","mae"),
  nrounds = 100,
  nfold = 5,
  showsd = TRUE,
  prediction = TRUE,
  early_stopping_rounds = 10, # stops at best iter
  verbose = 0
)

# Best cross-validated metrics across boosting rounds
cat("\n======= XGBoost Metrics =========")


======= XGBoost Metrics =========

cat("\nRMSE:", min(xgb_cv$evaluation_log$test_rmse_mean))


RMSE: 2.678364

cat("\nMAE:", min(xgb_cv$evaluation_log$test_mae_mean))


MAE: 1.974157

cat("\nRsquared:", cor(ml_data$incidence_rate, as.vector(xgb_cv$cv_predict$pred))^2)


Rsquared: 0.0003179616








NoteWhat cross-validation does



k-fold cross-validation splits the data into k parts, repeatedly trains on k−1 parts, and evaluates on the held-out part. Every row is predicted by a model that never saw it, so the resulting metric is an honest estimate of performance on new data — the opposite of the in-sample metrics above.

trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 5) does 5-fold CV repeated 5 times with different random splits (25 fits per candidate model), reducing the noise in the estimate.
method = "rf" and "svmRadial" are caret’s model codes for random forest and radial-kernel SVM. preProcess = c("center", "scale") scales predictors within each fold — done inside CV so scaling is not contaminated by the held-out data.
The latest xgboost has a compatibility issue with caret::train, so XGBoost is cross-validated directly with xgb.cv(). early_stopping_rounds halts training when the held-out error stops improving.



Key parameters: - trainControl() with "repeatedcv" performs 5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times with different random fold assignments each time. - method = "rf", "svmRadial" are caret’s standardised model-methods for random forest and SVM. - preProcess standardises the predictors within each fold for SVM.
Expected output: Cross-validated out-of-fold metrics for random forest and SVR (via caret::train) and for XGBoost (manually calculated).






NoteThe honest result



With no signal in the covariates, the cross-validated R² collapses toward zero for all three models (roughly 0.15 for RF, 0.07 for SVR, and ≈ 0 for XGBoost) — a stark contrast to the near-perfect in-sample fits. This collapse is the lesson: never trust a training-set score alone.

5.8 Identify Spatial Patterns and Risk Factors
Purpose: Use the trained models’ predictions to check whether any spatial pattern emerges, to inform health decision-making.

# Attach out-of-fold predictions back onto the spatial object
rf_oof <- rf_cv$pred |> 
  group_by(rowIndex) |> 
  summarise(pred_rf = mean(pred), .groups = "drop") |> 
  arrange(rowIndex)

svr_oof <- svr_cv$pred |> 
  group_by(rowIndex) |> 
  summarise(pred_svr = mean(pred), .groups = "drop") |> 
  arrange(rowIndex)

xgb_oof <- tibble(
  rowIndex = seq_len(nrow(ml_data)),
  pred_xgb = as.vector(xgb_cv$cv_predict$pred)
)

africa_health <- africa_health |> 
  mutate(
    pred_rf  = rf_oof$pred_rf,
    pred_xgb = xgb_oof$pred_xgb,
    pred_svr = svr_oof$pred_svr
  )

# Observed vs Predicted diagnostic plot via mlspatial
plot_obs_vs_pred(
  observed = africa_health$incidence_rate,
  predicted = africa_health$pred_rf,
  title = "Random Forest CV: Observed vs Predicted"
)







plot_obs_vs_pred(
  observed = africa_health$incidence_rate,
  predicted = africa_health$pred_svr,
  title = "SVR CV: Observed vs Predicted"
)







plot_obs_vs_pred(
  observed = africa_health$incidence_rate,
  predicted = africa_health$pred_xgb,
  title = "XGB CV: Observed vs Predicted"
)







# Map predictions vs observed
obs_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "incidence_rate",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Observed")
  ) +
  tm_borders() 

pred_rf_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "pred_rf",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted (RF)")
  ) +
  tm_borders() 

pred_xgb_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "pred_xgb",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted (XGB)")
  ) +
  tm_borders() 

pred_svr_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_fill(
    fill = "pred_svr",
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted (SVR)")
  ) +
  tm_borders() 

tmap_arrange(obs_map, pred_rf_map, pred_xgb_map, pred_svr_map, ncol = 2)














NoteReading this section




Out-of-fold predictions are the predictions made on each row while it was held out during CV. rf_cv$pred stores them; we group_by(rowIndex) and average over the repeated folds to get one prediction per country, then re-attach them to africa_health by row order (the same trick used to drop the geometry earlier).
plot_obs_vs_pred() draws observed vs predicted with a dashed 1:1 line: points hugging that line indicate a good model. For our signal-free data the points scatter widely around it.
The four maps compare the observed map with each model’s predicted map. If a model had learned a real spatial pattern, its predictions would reproduce the observed map’s structure.



Expected output: - A scatterplot with a 1:1 line and Pearson’s r. - Side-by-side maps showing how well the RF, XGB and SVR models reproduce spatial patterns.
Across every method in this module — Random Forest, XGBoost, SVR — the consistent finding is that our six simulated lifestyle/genetic covariates carry no real signal. This is the intended result of a teaching dataset: it demonstrates that the entire ML pipeline (data prep → training → tuning → evaluation → spatial pattern mapping) runs correctly and produces internally consistent, honestly interpreted null results. When you apply this exact pipeline to real covariate data in your own research, this is the standard of scrutiny that should accompany any reported results.

5.9 Practical Exercise
Consolidate the module with a few tasks, then check your answers against the solution.

Train a Random Forest with ntree = 200 and a different seed. Report the % variance explained.
Use xgb.importance() to list the top three predictors by Gain.
Compute the in-sample R² of the SVR model with postResample().
(Challenge) Re-run the caret random-forest cross-validation with number = 10 (10-fold) and compare the best RMSE with the 5-fold result above.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(mlspatial)
library(randomForest)
library(xgboost)
library(e1071)
library(caret)

data(africa_shp, package = "mlspatial")
data(panc_incidence, package = "mlspatial")
africa_health <- join_data(
  africa_shp |> mutate(NAME = gsub("Côte d'Ivoire", "Cote d'Ivoire", NAME)),
  panc_incidence, by = "NAME"
)
africa_health <- st_make_valid(africa_health)

set.seed(898)
n <- nrow(africa_health)
africa_health <- africa_health |>
  mutate(
    incidence_rate = (incidence / TOTPOP) * 100000,
    smoking_prev = round(runif(n, 8, 28), 1),
    obesity_prev = round(runif(n, 5, 30), 1),
    diabetes_prev = round(runif(n, 2, 11), 1),
    alcohol_per_capita = round(runif(n, 0.5, 12), 1),
    family_history_prev = round(runif(n, 3, 10), 1),
    urbanization_pct = round(runif(n, 15, 85), 1)
  )

ml_data <- africa_health |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(incidence_rate, smoking_prev, obesity_prev, diabetes_prev,
         alcohol_per_capita, family_history_prev, urbanization_pct, TOTPOP) |>
  drop_na()

rf_formula <- incidence_rate ~ smoking_prev + obesity_prev + diabetes_prev +
  alcohol_per_capita + family_history_prev + urbanization_pct + TOTPOP
predictors <- c("smoking_prev", "obesity_prev", "diabetes_prev",
                "alcohol_per_capita", "family_history_prev",
                "urbanization_pct", "TOTPOP")

# 1. Random forest with ntree = 200, new seed
rf2 <- train_rf(data = ml_data, formula = rf_formula, ntree = 200, seed = 4815)
tail(rf2$rsq, 1) * 100      # % variance explained (near 0)

# 2. Top-3 XGBoost predictors by Gain
set.seed(222)
xgb_model <- train_xgb(data = ml_data, formula = rf_formula,
                       nrounds = 100, max_depth = 4, learning_rate = 0.1)
xgb.importance(xgb_model) |> head(3)

# 3. In-sample SVR R-squared
ml_data_scaled <- ml_data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(predictors), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))
svr_model <- train_svr(data = ml_data, formula = rf_formula)
postResample(predict(svr_model, newdata = ml_data_scaled),
             ml_data$incidence_rate)["Rsquared"]

# 4. 10-fold RF cross-validation
set.seed(222)
cv10 <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 5,
                     savePredictions = "final")
rf_cv10 <- train(rf_formula, data = ml_data, method = "rf", trControl = cv10)
min(rf_cv10$results$RMSE)

6.1 Overlay Disease Burden with Service Availability
This final module brings everything together. You will overlay disease burden with health facility locations, calculate accessibility distances, generate reproducible reports, and reflect on the ethical dimensions of spatial epidemiology.
What you will learn
This module is the payoff of the whole tutorial: the earlier modules taught you how to import, map, model, and predict; this one shows you how those pieces combine into a decision-ready deliverable.
Purpose: Identify under-served areas by superimposing disease burden on health facility locations.
# Classify burden into tertiles (3 groups) for clearer visual communication
africa_health <- africa_health |>
  mutate(
    burden_class = case_when(
      incidence_rate >= quantile(incidence_rate, 0.67, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "High",
      incidence_rate >= quantile(incidence_rate, 0.33, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Medium",
      TRUE ~ "Low"
    ),
    burden_class = factor(burden_class, levels = c("High", "Medium", "Low"))
  )

# Simulate 70 health facility points across Africa for demonstration
set.seed(4607)
facility_points <- st_sample(africa_health, size = 70, type = "random") |> 
  st_as_sf() |> 
  mutate(facility_id = paste0("FAC_", row_number()),
         type = "Health Facilities")

decision_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_fill(
    "burden_class", 
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = c("High"="red","Medium"="yellow","Low"="green")),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Disease Burden", 
                            position = c("left", "bottom")) 
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(facility_points) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "type",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values ="darkblue"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Facilities", 
                            position = c("left", "bottom")),
    size = 0.4
  ) +
  tm_title("High Burden vs. Facility Coverage") 

decision_map

NoteHow the classification works




quantile(incidence_rate, 0.67) returns the value that splits the countries so that roughly two-thirds are below it and one-third above. case_when() then labels each country “High”, “Medium”, or “Low” against the 0.67 and 0.33 cut-points. With 54 countries this produces three groups of 18.
Converting burden_class to a factor(levels = c("High","Medium","Low")) fixes the legend order so “High” appears first.
st_sample(..., type = "random") drops 70 random points inside the polygons (reproducible thanks to set.seed(4607)), standing in for real health-facility coordinates.
The map itself layers the burden fill and the facility dots; red polygons with no nearby blue dots are the priority areas.

6.2 Distance / Accessibility Analysis
Purpose: Quantify the distance from each administrative unit to the nearest health facility.

# Transform both facility points and africa_health sf object to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
# This gives true geodesic distances with st_distance
africa_health_geo <- st_transform(africa_health, crs = 4326)
facility_points_geo <- st_transform(facility_points, crs = 4326)

# Calculate centroid of each polygon (using transformed data)
africa_centroids <- st_centroid(africa_health_geo, of_largest_polygon = TRUE)

# Matrix of geodesic distances (meters) between centroids and facility points
dist_matrix <- st_distance(africa_centroids, facility_points_geo)

# Minimum distance per country (convert to km) and append to original dataset
africa_health <- africa_health |>
  mutate(
    dist_to_facility_km = as.numeric(apply(dist_matrix, 1, min)) / 1000
  )

# Summary statistics
summary(africa_health$dist_to_facility_km)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  31.32  220.03  272.47  357.79  457.92 1522.73 

# Map accessibility
access_map <- tm_shape(africa_health) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "dist_to_facility_km", 
    fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "brewer.bu_pu"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Distance (km)")
        ) +
  tm_shape(facility_points) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "type",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values ="red"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Facility"),
    size = 0.4
  ) +
  tm_title("Distance to Nearest Health Facility")

access_map














NoteHow the distance pipeline works




st_centroid(..., of_largest_polygon = TRUE) places one point at the centre of each country (using the largest piece for multi-part countries such as island nations).
st_distance(africa_centroids, facility_points_geo) returns a matrix with one row per country and one column per facility — cell (i, j) is the distance from country i to facility j. Here that is a 54 × 70 matrix.
apply(dist_matrix, 1, min) takes the minimum along each row, i.e. the distance from each country to its nearest facility. Dividing by 1000 converts metres to kilometres.
The map then shades countries by that nearest-facility distance — the classic accessibility map used to plan service placement.









WarningCRS and Geodesic Distances



When calculating distances, it is crucial to know your CRS. Because our data was transformed to EPSG:4326 (WGS 84), the sf package uses spherical maths to calculate accurate, real-world geodesic distances, returning the results in metres. Dividing by 1000 gives us kilometres.








NoteProjected CRS for local analysis



While the spherical engine handles distance perfectly, if you are doing highly localized spatial modelling or calculating exact polygon areas in Ghana, it is still best practice to reproject your data to a metric coordinate system like UTM Zone 30N (EPSG:32630).


Expected output: - Summary statistics of distance (here the median is around 346 km, ranging from roughly 29 km to 2,380 km). - A map showing increasing distance as darker purple fills.

6.3 Result Interpretation and Report Generation
Purpose: Produce a reproducible, shareable document integrating code, results, and narrative.
A reproducible report is one where the text, numbers, tables, and figures are all generated from code, so a colleague (or future you) can re-run it and get identical results. R Markdown (.Rmd) and Quarto (.qmd) are the gold standards for reproducible research. Below is a minimal Quarto document skeleton you can adapt:
---
title: "Spatial Epidemiology Report: Pancreatic Cancer in Africa"
format: html
editor: visual
---

## Introduction
This report analyzes the spatial distribution ...

## Data
```r
#| echo: false
library(mlspatial)
data(africa_shp)
data(panc_incidence)
```

## Results
The Global Moran's I was 0.074 (inserted via inline code) ...

## Conclusion
High-burden hotspots are concentrated in ...






NoteThe three ingredients of a reproducible report




Code chunks (```{r}) run when the document is rendered, so every figure and table is regenerated from the current data.
Inline code embeds an R expression directly in a sentence (wrapped in backticks and prefixed with the letter r), so computed numbers update automatically when the data changes instead of being typed by hand.
Parameterised reports use a params: block in the YAML header to produce, say, one country report per country from a single template.



Key features: - Code chunks (```{r}) execute during rendering. - Inline code embeds R expressions in the text, updating numbers automatically. - Parameterised reports: Use YAML params: to generate country-specific reports from one template.
Expected output: An HTML or PDF file containing embedded maps, tables, and narrative — fully reproducible by any colleague who has the .qmd file and data.

6.4 Ethical Considerations
Purpose: Reflect on methodological biases and data privacy before disseminating findings.
Spatial epidemiology maps people, not just polygons. Before publishing, it is worth pausing to consider how a map can help — or harm — the communities it describes.

6.4.1 Privacy Protection

Aggregated data: The mlspatial built-in data are already aggregated to country level, protecting individual identity. Never map exact household locations or small-area counts (< 5 cases) without differential privacy or aggregation.
Re-identification risk: Combining spatial coordinates with demographic details (age, sex, date of diagnosis) can re-identify patients in small villages.



6.4.2 Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)

Definition: Results depend on the boundaries chosen. Country-level analysis may hide sub-national hotspots; conversely, fine-scale analysis may produce unstable rates due to small populations.
Mitigation: Conduct sensitivity analyses at multiple scales (district, region, country) and report how conclusions change.



6.4.3 Ecological Fallacy

Definition: Relationships observed at the aggregate level do not necessarily hold for individuals. For example, a country with high average temperature and high cancer incidence does not prove that heat causes cancer in individual patients.
Mitigation: Use language like “areas with higher temperature are associated with higher incidence” rather than “temperature causes cancer.”



6.4.4 Spatial Inequality & Resource Allocation

Maps are political. Highlighting “high burden” regions can attract funding, but it can also stigmatize communities. Always:

Share results with local health officials before publication.
Provide confidence intervals or classification uncertainty.
Pair burden maps with resource maps (as in Section 6.1) to focus on actionable gaps.

data(panc_incidence, package = "mlspatial")
africa_health <- join_data(
  africa_shp |> mutate(NAME = gsub("Côte d'Ivoire", "Cote d'Ivoire", NAME)),
  panc_incidence, by = "NAME"
)
africa_health <- st_make_valid(africa_health)

set.seed(898)
n <- nrow(africa_health)
africa_health <- africa_health |>
  mutate(incidence_rate = (incidence / TOTPOP) * 100000)

# 1. Quartile classification
africa_health <- africa_health |>
  mutate(burden_q = case_when(
    incidence_rate >= quantile(incidence_rate, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Q4",
    incidence_rate >= quantile(incidence_rate, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Q3",
    incidence_rate >= quantile(incidence_rate, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Q2",
    TRUE ~ "Q1"
  ))
table(africa_health$burden_q)

# 2. Nearest-facility distance
set.seed(4607)
facility_points <- st_sample(africa_health, size = 70, type = "random") |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  mutate(facility_id = paste0("FAC_", row_number()))

centroids <- st_centroid(st_transform(africa_health, 4326),
                         of_largest_polygon = TRUE)
d <- st_distance(centroids, st_transform(facility_points, 4326))
africa_health$dist_km <- as.numeric(apply(d, 1, min)) / 1000

summary(africa_health$dist_km)          # median and max

# 3. Country farthest from a facility
africa_health$NAME[which.max(africa_health$dist_km)]
